Canada wants to become the European Union's first “associate member” by June 2027

At the EU-Canada summit in Montreal (October 29-30), Prime Minister Mark Carney set a goal: to conclude negotiations by June 2027 on an unprecedented link with the Union, halfway between partner and member. Yet the word “associate” disappeared from the final declaration after Germany objected [2][6].

At the 21st EU-Canada summit, held in Montreal on October 29 and 30, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he wants to conclude negotiations by June 2027 to make Canada the European Union's first “associate member” [1][2][6].

He spoke of “the deepest possible partnership short of membership, because of our geography”; yet the word “associate” does not appear in the summit's final declaration, as Germany had objected a few hours before the European delegation arrived in Montreal [2][3].

The text signed with António Costa, President of the European Council, and Ursula von der Leyen, President of the Commission, commits both sides to work toward an “ever closer association” and to define the concept by the next summit, in 2027, without full membership [6].
The idea comes from Ursula von der Leyen, who proposed it on September 16 in her State of the Union speech [4]. Carney promised debates, then a vote, in the Canadian Parliament [2][3].

On October 30, Brussels and Ottawa also concluded negotiations on a digital trade agreement, presented on the Canadian side as the country's first one devoted entirely to the subject: it sets rules on data flows, electronic signatures and contracts, and online commerce [7].
This agreement complements CETA, the EU-Canada free trade agreement provisionally applied since 2017 [7].
Key takeaway: this is a status that does not yet exist. It will have to be invented, accepted by the Union's 27 countries, and put to a vote by the Canadian Parliament [2][3].

The summit shows the gap between ambition and text: leaders talk about an associate member, but the declaration only retains “ever closer association,” and the precise definition is pushed back to 2027 [2][6]. Member states did not all agree, with Germany leading the objections [2][3].

For Canada, it is a way to depend less on its large American neighbor, amid a trade war with Washington [3]. For Europe, it is one more ally at a time when its relations with the United States are strained [3].

An associate member, however, would have no European citizenship, no free movement, no commissioner and no voting rights in the Union's institutions [5]. What is concretely moving forward until then are sector-specific agreements, such as digital trade [7].

Nothing changes for you in the short term: CETA has applied since 2017 [7], and the associate status remains to be defined. If the project succeeds, exchanges between Europe and Canada would become even simpler: goods, studies, work, defense. Above all, it is one more sign that alliances are being redrawn in response to American trade policy [3][5].
Both sides must define the concept of “ever closer association” by the next EU-Canada summit [6].

Venezuela: opposition leader Machado returns from exile and demands elections, criticizing the oil deal with the United States

María Corina Machado, Nobel Peace Prize laureate, returned to Venezuela on October 25 after more than ten months in exile. On the 29th, she called for elections in 2027 and judged the oil deal struck with the United States by interim president Delcy Rodríguez too opaque; Rodríguez promises a vote with no date [1][4][6].
María Corina Machado, Nobel Peace Prize laureate, returned to Venezuela on October 25, 2026 after more than ten months in exile [1][4][5].

On October 29, at her first press conference at the Andrés Bello Catholic University in Caracas, she called for elections in 2027 and thanked the Trump administration for the January 3 operation that removed Nicolás Maduro, which she said opened a “gateway to freedom” [1].
She criticizes the oil deal: “This agreement does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants,” she said, adding that she had not seen the contract [1].
Al Jazeera describes a deal that would hand over 20% of the country's oil reserves [1]; the Rio Times writes that the Pentagon holds 35% of it and that the contract is not public [7].
A first million barrels of Venezuelan crude arrived in Corpus Christi (Texas) on October 27, aboard two tankers; Donald Trump welcomed the delivery [3][7].
Delcy Rodríguez says the elections will be organized by a “renewed electoral authority,” in line with the Constitution, but without setting a date [1][6].
Key takeaway: Machado is not opposing Washington, she thanks Donald Trump, but she wants a date for the vote and publication of the oil contract [1].

Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro's former vice president, has run the country since his capture by the United States in January, and NPR notes that many Venezuelans reject her because of her role under Maduro [1][6].

Washington is also pushing for an election: Secretary of State Marco Rubio wants a nonpartisan Supreme Court and electoral council in place within a few months, then Rodríguez's departure and a vote within six months; he says he judges the leader “by her actions” [6].
The two issues are linked: oil is already flowing to Texas, while neither the date of the vote nor the contents of the contract are known [1][3][7].
More Venezuelan oil on the market can help calm energy prices, but the deal raises questions of democracy and transparency. As long as the contract stays secret, it is unclear who benefits [1][3][7].

news.2026-10-31-portugal-logement-manife: Portugal: thousands protest for housing outside Parliament, amid budget debate
On October 27, thousands of people demonstrated outside Parliament in Lisbon, at the start of the debate on the 2027 budget, which was passed on first reading on the 28th [1][3][4].

The previous Sunday, police dismantled activist camps in Lisbon and Porto: 11 people lightly injured, including 3 police officers, according to police; 60 according to the Casa para Viver collective [3].
They oppose easier evictions and the end of rent caps on new leases [3]. According to the national statistics institute, housing prices rose by almost 20% between early 2025 and early 2026 [1].
Prime Minister Luís Montenegro considers the police action consistent with “necessity, proportionality and adequacy” [3]; President António José Seguro condemned the violence [5].

On October 28, the budget passed on first reading despite 79 votes against, thanks to 60 abstentions, 58 of them Socialist. PS leader José Luís Carneiro says the country cannot enter a political crisis [4][6]. The government highlights wages [2].
Key takeaway: housing is a major social grievance in Portugal, and the street is weighing on a minority government that only gets by thanks to the PS [1][4].
The final vote takes place on November 24, after committee work [4][6]. Seguro has convened the Council of State [3].
Lisbon attracts tourists and foreigners, which pushes up rents: a debate also present in France [1].

news.2026-10-31-france-pib-recule-t3.tit: France contracts in the third quarter while the eurozone holds up
news.2026-10-31-france-pib-recule-t3.sum: French GDP fell 0.1% between July and September, after stagnating in the spring, while economists had expected a slight rise. Meanwhile, the eurozone grew 0.4%: foreign trade, notably aerospace, is dragging France down [1][5][6][7].
news.2026-10-31-france-pib-recule-t3.poi: According to Insee's first estimate, published on October 30, France's GDP fell 0.1% in the third quarter, after 0.0% in the second and −0.2% in the first; economists had expected a slight rise [1][2][3][5].
Foreign trade weighs the most: it subtracts 0.6 points from growth, after adding 0.6 in the spring; exports fell 1.7%, with a sharp decline in aerospace [2][5][7].
Household consumption rose 0.4%, supported notably by purchases of electric cars after the surge in fuel prices [2][5][7]. Public spending increased 0.3% [7].
Investment fell again, by 0.6% after −0.5%: −0.4% for businesses, −1.3% for households and −0.3% for public administrations [2][5][7].

Meanwhile, the eurozone grew 0.4% (versus 0.6% in the second quarter) and the EU 0.5%; Germany rose 0.2%, Spain 0.6%, and Italy stayed at 0.0% [3][4][6]. Only Lithuania did worse than France (−1.0%) [6].

Roland Lescure, the economy minister, attributes the shortfall to a drop in agricultural output hit by the heat wave and to lower energy production; he argues for "restoring confidence" by adopting a budget [1][7].
news.2026-10-31-france-pib-recule-t3.why: Key takeaway: France is lagging behind its neighbors just as it has to vote on a tight budget [1][3].

The minister says the economy "has come to a standstill" and "will hit a wall" without fiscal consolidation, and calls for a compromise in Parliament [1][7]. The government is still counting on 0.5% growth in 2026; yet the carry-over effect, what the year would already have if activity stayed flat until December, is only 0.2% [1][5][7].
Falling GDP means less wealth produced, and therefore less revenue for the state, while the deficit is already high. The Banque de France had nevertheless forecast a rise of about 0.1% [2].
This is only a first estimate: Eurostat will publish a new estimate on November 13, and Insee its detailed results on November 27 [5][6].
news.2026-10-31-france-pib-recule-t3.for: A stalling economy weighs on jobs and on the budget's room for maneuver: it is one more argument in the debates on taxes and spending in the coming weeks. At your level, household consumption is holding up (+0.4%), but investment by businesses and households continues to fall [1][2][5].
news.2026-10-31-france-pib-recule-t3.nex: Eurostat publishes a new estimate of eurozone growth [6].

Cambodia: almost half as many foreign tourists as a year ago

Cambodia welcomed 2.46 million foreign tourists from January to September 2026, versus 4.38 million a year earlier, or 43.7% fewer. According to Tourism Minister Huot Hak, online scam networks, tensions with Thailand and expensive fuel explain the decline [1][2].
On October 27, 2026, the Ministry of Tourism published a tally of 2,464,033 foreign tourists from January to September, versus 4,377,466 over the same period in 2025, or −43.7% [1][2].

Vietnam remains the top market with 651,486 visitors (−28%), ahead of China with 643,314 (−27.6%); Americans fell by only 5.6%, to 140,276 [1][2]. Vietnam has thus overtaken China as the leading source of visitors [3].

Minister Huot Hak attributes the drop to bad publicity linked to online scam networks, friction at the border with Thailand and conflicts in the Middle East, which pushed up fuel prices and dampened the desire to travel [1][2].
The decline has lasted for months: the cumulative figure was −44.4% over the first eight months of 2026 [5], and is −43.7% over nine months [1][2].

At Angkor, 510,528 foreign visitors bought a ticket from January to September, 27.6% fewer than a year earlier; ticket revenue reaches $24.23 million (−25.9%) [4]. The site is therefore falling less than the country as a whole [1][4].
Official sources speak of "friction" at the Thai border, without detailing its effect on arrivals by road [1][2].
Key takeaway: a drop of more than 40% in nine months is a shock for a country where tourism is a pillar of the economy, and it hits hotels, guides and businesses around Angkor [1][2][4].

The minister cites three causes, but the sources do not say how much each contributed to the decline [1][2]. What is measured is the gap by country of origin: the two big Asian neighbors lose more than a quarter of their visitors, Americans a little over one twentieth [1][2].
The link with the war around Hormuz runs through fuel: according to the minister, the conflict in the Middle East pushed up its price and curbed the desire to travel worldwide [1][2].
The ministry publishes its figures every month (eight months, then nine months), which makes it possible to track whether the annual cumulative figure stabilizes [1][5].

The fuel price tied to the war around Hormuz is spilling over into travel in Southeast Asia, and therefore into the destinations you can consider. If you plan to visit Angkor, be aware that the site is receiving markedly fewer foreigners than before [1][2][4].

Nigeria: Dangote refinery's stock market listing draws about three times the targeted amount

The share offering of the Dangote refinery, in Lagos, closed on October 27 after 44 days. According to Reuters, citing sources, orders reach about 6.4 trillion naira ($4.78 billion), nearly three times the target. Allocation and listing are yet to come.
The public share offering of the Dangote refinery opened on September 14 and closed on October 27, 2026, a 44-day window, after a two-week extension granted to broaden participation [3][5].
The offering covers 4.1 billion new shares at 525 naira each, or 2.15 trillion naira (about $1.6 billion) [4].
According to Reuters, citing two sources, orders reach about 6.4 trillion naira ($4.78 billion), nearly three times the target [1][4].
Aliko Dangote, the group's founder, himself says demand reached three to four times the target [3].
An over-allotment option could take the deal beyond $2.1 billion, and small retail investors would be served first [1][2].
Investors from about 119 countries subscribed, according to Legit.ng [5].

Final subscription and allocation figures had not yet been published; the listing on the Lagos stock exchange, originally targeted for November, would now be expected in December according to Legit.ng [5].
Key takeaway: this IPO would be one of the largest in Africa, driven by investor appetite for local refining [1][2].

When an offering is oversubscribed, demand exceeds the available securities: investors only get part of what they asked for, and the priority promised to small retail investors affects the split [1][2].
The $4.78 billion figure comes from anonymous sources cited by Reuters, not from an official statement: the allocation announcement must be awaited to confirm it [1][4].
Demand exceeds the target by a factor of about 2.98 (6.4 divided by 2.15), which matches the phrase "nearly three times" used by the media [1][4].

A giant African refiner reduces the continent's dependence on imported fuel, which matters when oil is expensive. This news item explains how an IPO works and does not constitute investment advice [1][2].

Paris: curfews over the All Saints' Day weekend after the October looting

The Paris police prefecture bans unaccompanied minors from going out at night in several Paris neighborhoods, and everyone at République and Les Halles, from October 30 to November 2. It cites the October looting and risks of violence. An earlier curfew on minors had been suspended by the courts [1][2][3][4].
One curfew targets unaccompanied minors in several areas of Paris, from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m., from Friday evening to Monday morning, November 2 [1][2][6].

A second order bans everyone from being present, from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m., on Place de la République and in the Châtelet-Les Halles area, from October 31 to November 2 [2][3][6]. The prefecture cites risks of violence and calls to commit acts of vandalism [2][6].

On October 28, the Paris administrative court suspended the earlier curfew on minors (9 p.m.–6 a.m., Monday to Thursday), following a challenge by the association Vigie Liberté; the judge faulted the prefect for giving no specific evidence of risks linked to minors on those days and at those hours [3][4]. That measure ran from October 26 to 29 [3].
The prefecture relies on the looting and damage of October 17 and 18: on the night of the 18th, Paris was again targeted by looters after the October 17 mobilization [3][7].

On October 24, the Paris march went off largely peacefully, but the prefecture counted 142 arrests, including 126 held in custody; turnout is estimated at between 110,000 and 250,000 people depending on the source [3][5]. A curfew had already been imposed around the Forum des Halles and Place de la République after October 17 [5].
After an inter-ministerial crisis meeting, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu asked prefects for “partial” and highly localized curfews [1][6].
Key point: this is a rare measure in the capital, taken after several weeks of tension [2][3].

The legal stakes are central: a curfew restricts freedom of movement, and the administrative judge already ruled on October 28 that the prefecture had not justified the first version targeting minors [3][4]. The new orders will therefore have to stand on their justification, in particular the risks linked to calls to commit acts of vandalism [2][6].

The choice of very limited zones, République and Châtelet-Les Halles, matches Matignon's instruction for “partial” and “localized” curfews [1][6]. These are also the areas already placed under curfew after the October 17 mobilization [5].
New legal challenges can still be brought before the courts [2].

If you are in Paris this weekend, check the affected streets on the police prefecture's website before going out late: at République and Les Halles, being present is banned from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m., and unaccompanied minors cannot go out from 9 p.m. in several neighborhoods [2][3][6].

Hormuz: Iran says three tankers hit mines, Washington denies it

Iran's Revolutionary Guards say three tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz; US Central Command (Centcom) says no ship has hit one. October nonetheless has twice as many attacks as September, and Brent closed at $117.64 [1][2][6].

The Revolutionary Guards say three tankers, including a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels, hit mines and caught fire on the southern routes of the strait on October 29 and 30; these claims could not be independently confirmed [2][7].
Centcom replied on X that “no ship has hit a mine” in the strait and that all the main internationally recognized transit routes have been cleared of mines by US forces [2][6].
CNBC counts twice as many ship attacks in October as in September, when 15 incidents were confirmed; that is more than any other month of the war [1].
According to Kpler, the cost of shipping crude rose to about $21 a barrel, versus $6.50 in September [1].

Crude exports through Hormuz averaged nearly 11.1 million barrels a day in October (about 2% below September), but only 7.3 million in the week ending Wednesday the 28th, more than 40% below the pre-war level [1].
The December Brent contract, which expired on October 30, closed at $117.64, close to the war's record ($118.35 in March); Brent gained 13.6% over the month and WTI 15% [1][4][5].
Key point: even under attack, tankers keep passing, but in smaller numbers, and the market is paying for it [1].

The mechanism is cost: when risk rises, shipping costs more, and CNBC quotes an analyst saying this is “starting to weigh on margins” for refiners. Some operators are now sending their own ships to brave the passage [1].

The dispute over the mines is a contested claim: Iran says so, Washington denies it, and no independent source settles it [2][6][7]. What is established is the drop in flows over the last week, from 11.1 to 7.3 million barrels a day [1].
On prices, Brent is less than a dollar below its March high ($117.64 versus $118.35) after a 13.6% rise in October: the oil market is reacting to risk, even before flows collapse [1][4][5].

Expensive oil shows up at the pump and on your heating bill: the tension in Hormuz directly affects your budget. The more flows fall and the more shipping costs, the more likely the rise is to last [1][3].

news.2026-10-31-espagne-pib-inflation-t3: Spain still grows 0.6%, but inflation stays near 5%
Spain's statistics institute (INE) published a first estimate on October 30: GDP grew 0.6% in the third quarter, a tenth less than in the second, and inflation stays at 4.9% in October [1][4].
Spanish GDP grew 0.6% over the quarter, after 0.7% in the second, and 2.7% over a year, versus 2.6% in the previous quarter [1][2][4].
On a quarterly basis, domestic demand contributes 0.5 points of growth and external demand 0.1 points; consumption and investment slow, while public spending accelerates to 0.9% [4][6].
Annual inflation stays at 4.9% in October, as in September, the third month in a row above 4%; core inflation is 3.1% [1][7][8].
According to INE, fuel prices are falling more than a year ago, which holds the index down; gas, more expensive than a year ago, pushes it up [7][8].
Key point: Spain remains one of the most dynamic economies in the euro area, well ahead of France (−0.1%) [1][2].

Inflation at 4.9% complicates the task of the European Central Bank, which sets a single rate for the whole euro area and left its deposit rate at 2.5% on October 29 [11]. Italy is at 5.4% and Germany at 2.8% [9].
If you travel or shop in Spain, prices there are rising faster than in France right now [1][3].
The ECB holds its last monetary policy meeting of the year, with new economic projections [10].

Poland: the president turns his plane around to defend the head of the Constitutional Court

On Friday 30 October, judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska suspended the president of Poland's Constitutional Court, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy. The Court rejects the decision, police intervened, and President Karol Nawrocki cut short his trip to Senegal to go to the scene [1][2][3].

On the evening of Friday 30 October, judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska ordered a "pause in activity" for the Court's president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański; she accuses the former of repeatedly breaking the law [1][2].

According to TVN24, the order relies on Article 130 of the law on the organisation of ordinary courts, which is disputed: the Court says Święczkowski remains president and Sochański vice-president [5].

Police and the State Protection Service were outside the building and Święczkowski was not allowed in; protesters cut the chain on a gate, and Jarosław Kaczyński (PiS) and Piotr Gliński entered the grounds [5].

President Karol Nawrocki, on his way to a state visit to Senegal, had his plane turn back, helped the judge get in and entered the Court himself, accompanied by Zbigniew Kapiński, first president of the Supreme Court [2][3][5].
His office denounces a violation of the constitutional order and a takeover by force of a constitutional body; PiS and the Court speak of a "coup", which the government camp disputes [2][4].
Justice Minister and Prosecutor General Waldemar Żurek filed requests to lift the immunity of Święczkowski and Sochański [5].
The night also saw 3 protesters detained [2].
Key takeaway: two Polish camps are fighting over the leadership of the country's highest court, and no one yet knows who legally runs it [1][2].

The conflict dates back to 2015: the outgoing PO-PSL coalition had five judges elected by Parliament before the October 2015 parliamentary elections, and PiS then imposed its own appointments [4]. In December 2024, President Andrzej Duda appointed Święczkowski, a former prosecutor close to Zbigniew Ziobro, to head the Court [4].

Today, the government camp considers these appointments and this leadership irregular, while Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of the eight new judges elected by Parliament [3][4]. The sources do not settle the legality of the suspension; judge Korwin-Piotrowska's authority to take over the leadership is itself debated [1][5].

Poland carries weight in the European Union: if the Court that rules on laws is paralysed, rule-of-law rulings, and decisions taken among the 27, may become more complicated. Keep in mind 3 November, which will show whether the Court sits again [2][4].

India wants to build its own shipping containers: ten times more within a few years

On 28 October 2026, India's cabinet approved a 10,000-crore rupee plan (about $1 billion) to manufacture shipping containers in India. The goal: to go from about 70,000 to 750,000 TEU a year, under a programme running from 2027-28 to 2039-40 [1][2][4][5].

India's Union cabinet approved on Wednesday 28 October 2026 the "Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme" (CMPS), with a budget of 10,000 crore rupees, originally announced in the budget presented in February by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman [1][4][5].
Annual manufacturing capacity is to rise from about 70,000 TEU (twenty-foot equivalent units) to 750,000 TEU [1][5].

The envelope is split as follows: 8,891 crore for operating support, 859 crore for subsidised loan interest (3% a year on eligible term loans), 150 crore for testing and certification, 100 crore for management and training [1][4][5].
Manufacturers receive 49,500 rupees per 20-foot container produced and sold, and 86,625 rupees per 40-foot container [4][5].
A new plant must produce at least 100,000 TEU a year; an existing plant must add at least 25,000 TEU [1][5].
The plan runs from 2027-28 to 2039-40: three years to build the plants, then ten years of production support [1][2].
Estimates point to about 3,000 direct jobs and more than 50,000 indirect jobs [4][5].
Key takeaway: India wants to stop importing a basic link of global trade, the container, as its ports and exports grow [1][3].
The mechanism is a per-unit payment: support is paid only for containers actually produced and sold, which avoids funding plants that sit idle [4][5].
The capacity thresholds (100,000 TEU for a new plant) target industrial-scale sites rather than small workshops: at 100,000 TEU per site, reaching 750,000 TEU requires several plants [1][5].
The programme spans 13 years: the effect on freight prices will therefore not be seen before construction is finished, scheduled after three years [1][2].

Almost everything you buy has travelled in a container: who makes them, and at what price, affects the long-term cost of sea freight and the dependence of supply chains, but this plan should not change your prices for several years [1][3][5].

Africa: Ethiopia and Zambia open gold refineries to keep value at home

Ethiopia and Zambia opened their first gold refineries in October, to sell pure metal rather than ore or raw gold. Both countries follow Burkina Faso, but analysts say supply and certification remain the real tests.

Ethiopia inaugurated its first precious metals refinery on 10 October, in the Bole Lemi special economic zone near Addis Ababa: $50 million in investment, an announced capacity of more than 600 tonnes of precious metals a year, and majority state ownership [1][2].
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced the launch on 12 October and said the refinery will also process gold from Ethiopia and elsewhere, notably neighbouring countries [1][2].
Gold is Ethiopia's top export: $5.6 billion over the previous year, according to Reuters [1].

Zambia presented the Minera Refineries Zambia Limited refinery in late October at the Mining and Investment Insaka fair in Lusaka: it claims to reach about 99% purity, and its laboratory 99.99% [3][4].
Chief executive Andrew Mukupa Katandula proposes a two-year plan: formalise artisanal gold mining, offer targeted pre-financing to miners and better track gold sales [3][4].
Burkina Faso opened Raffinor BF in Ouagadougou in September, with an initial capacity of 164 tonnes a year and a second phase planned to reach 515 tonnes [5].
Key takeaway: refining locally earns more than selling raw gold, and can limit smuggling, since the gold goes through a controlled channel [1][4].
Ethiopia's capacity far exceeds its own output: the refinery will only run at full capacity if it processes gold from other countries [1][2].
For Zambia, supply is the main constraint: the plant must capture enough gold from artisanal miners to run profitably, hence the formalisation plan [3][4].

Analysts say owning a refinery guarantees neither profits nor control of the value chain: financing and international certification remain obstacles, and Guinea, for its part, has banned raw gold exports [4][5].

Gold serves as a safe-haven asset and goes into electronics: where it is refined decides who captures the wealth in the chain. This African movement may therefore, over time, change the metal's supply routes [4].

Azerbaijan's prime minister in Georgia: transport and energy on the South Caucasus agenda

Azerbaijani Prime Minister Ali Asadov made a two-day working visit to Georgia (October 29-30). With his counterpart Irakli Kobakhidze, he co-chaired the 11th joint economic commission in Sighnaghi and signed the session's protocol, along with agreements on a border crossing point and food safety [1][3][5][6].
Ali Asadov arrived in Tbilisi on October 29 for a two-day working visit [1][3].

On October 30, he held one-on-one talks with Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze in Sighnaghi, in the Kakheti region; Civil.ge places the meeting in Tbilisi, but APA, Report.az and Trend say Sighnaghi [2][4][6][7].
The two heads of government co-chaired the 11th session of the intergovernmental commission on economic cooperation and signed its protocol [5][6].
The agenda covered trade, energy, infrastructure and Middle Corridor projects, and both sides agreed to speed up the demarcation and delimitation of the border [7].
An agreement on the operation of the "Silk Road – Ipek Yolu" road border crossing was signed, along with documents on customs cooperation [5][7].
Two memorandums were signed by the Azerbaijan Food Safety Agency and Georgia's National Food Agency: one on plant quarantine, the other on veterinary services [5][7].
According to Asadov, Azerbaijan is the largest investor in Georgia, with almost 4 billion dollars invested [7][8].

Key takeaway: the meeting deals with very concrete issues (border, customs, transport, energy) between two neighbors that are also links in the Middle Corridor, the freight route connecting Asia to Europe [1][7].
The figure to remember is Azerbaijani investment in Georgia, almost 4 billion dollars according to Asadov, an amount that Civil.ge also reports and that is announced by the Azerbaijani side [7][8].
The memorandums on plant quarantine and veterinary services aim to ease trade in agricultural products at the border; the sources consulted do not give details of the customs documents [5][7].
The transport and energy agreements in the South Caucasus concern freight routes between Asia and Europe, and therefore, over time, the delivery times and costs of what arrives in Europe [1][7].

news.2026-10-31-vietnam-banques-etat-65-: Vietnam wants to keep its largest banks under state control

Vietnam has approved a plan to restructure public capital for 2026-2030 covering 21 enterprises. In the three big banks BIDV, Vietcombank and VietinBank, the state must keep at least 65% of the capital by 2030; Agribank remains 100% state-owned [1][2][5].
The plan, reportedly approved by Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang and made public on October 28, 2026, covers 21 state-owned or state-funded enterprises for the 2026-2030 period [2][4][5].
For BIDV, Vietcombank and VietinBank, the minimum state share is set at 65% by 2030 [1][2][3].
BIDV (76.73% today) and Vietcombank (74.8%) could therefore see the state share fall to 65%; VietinBank is the only one that must rise, from 64.46% to 65%, i.e. 0.54 points more [4][5].
The text does not say how these targets will be met; the Ministry of Finance and the State Bank of Vietnam are in charge of implementation [4][5].
The plan also provides for raising the state's stake in Vietnam Airlines from 39.29% to 86.42% [5].
Key takeaway: while many countries are selling stakes in their banks, Hanoi is setting a floor to keep control over credit in its economy [1][2].
The 65% floor leaves some room: the state can sell about ten points of BIDV and Vietcombank, for example by opening their capital to investors, while keeping control [4][5].
Controlling the banks makes it possible to steer loans toward sectors deemed strategic, but limits the role of private and foreign investors in their capital [1][2].
The plan goes beyond banks: Vietnam is also raising the public stake in its airline, which shows a logic of control over groups deemed strategic [1][5].
Vietnam has become a workshop of the world for electronics and textiles: how it finances its factories indirectly affects the products you buy, even if this plan has no direct effect on you [1][2].

news.2026-10-31-perou-fujimori-prison-sa: Peru wants to copy El Salvador's mega-prison: Keiko Fujimori visits CECOT

Peru's president, Keiko Fujimori, visited CECOT, El Salvador's mega-prison, on October 29, then met Nayib Bukele. She announces two new prisons in Peru, one inspired by CECOT, with no published cost or timeline. NGOs warn about the human cost of the model.

Keiko Fujimori, president of Peru, visited the CECOT (Terrorism Confinement Center) on Thursday, October 29, the maximum-security prison built by Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, during a four-day official trip to El Salvador [1][4].
The trip also included a bilateral summit with Nayib Bukele; according to Latin Times, it produced cooperation agreements covering public security, prison management and crime prevention [2][4].
After the visit, she announced that Peru would build two new prisons: one for the most dangerous inmates, modeled on CECOT, the other for inmates considered less dangerous [3][4].
She said the visit "will inspire us a great deal to be able to replicate these prisons," in connection with six prisons already under construction in Peru, which would incorporate Bukele's model [4].
The Salvadoran proposals will be assessed under Peruvian law; neither the budget, the sites nor the dates of the new prisons were specified in the articles consulted [3][4].

Peru's prison system is overcrowded: data from the INPE, the prison administration, indicate about 150% occupancy in 2026, and the army guards the perimeter of five prisons placed under emergency [5].
Key takeaway: the "Bukele model" is increasingly appealing to Latin American leaders facing crime, and Keiko Fujimori is the latest to visit CECOT [1][2].
CECOT became famous when the Trump administration sent more than 250 deported Venezuelans there, accused of gang ties, without evidence being presented [1].
Human rights organizations warn that this model has a documented human cost, linked to mass detentions and conditions of confinement; they are already monitoring the Peruvian projects [2].

On the Peruvian side, the debate centers on adapting the model to national law and on the real capacity to fund and build: the full text of the signed agreements has not been published, and what comes next has yet to be dated [3][4][5].

Security has become a major electoral issue in the region, and choices made in Lima or San Salvador influence debates elsewhere. If you follow Latin America, keep in mind that the announcement is an intention: no budget or timeline has been published yet [1][2][3].

news.2026-10-31-italie-croissance-nulle-: Italy at a standstill in Q3, with inflation at its highest in more than three years
On October 30, Istat published stable GDP for the third quarter, below expectations, and inflation of 5.4% in October, driven by energy [1][2][5].
According to Istat's preliminary estimate, Italian GDP did not grow in the third quarter compared with the second, slightly worse than expected; year on year, it gains 0.8% [1][4][5].
Services and agriculture grew, industry declined; net foreign trade weighed on growth [4][5].

Inflation reached 5.4% year on year in October versus 4.2% in September (+0.9% month on month), its highest level since August 2023 [2][3][6]. Energy prices jumped 31.4% year on year (22.6% in September) and regulated energy prices 59.5%, with Istat pointing to the geopolitical context [6].
Contractual wages rose more slowly than prices in the second and third quarters [7].
Key takeaway: Italy is an exception among the large European countries with this acceleration in prices, just as its growth stalls; the eurozone is advancing mainly thanks to Spain [1][2][7].
Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti says that "wars weigh on energy" and calls this impact worrying [8].
A stalled Italy means fewer orders for French companies, for which it is one of the biggest customers [1][2].
Istat publishes its next preliminary GDP estimate [4].
news.2026-10-31-kirghizistan-reseau-elec: Central Asia: winter threatens Soviet-era power grids, Kyrgyzstan freezes crypto mining

Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov has announced that no new cryptocurrency mining licenses will be granted until electricity production has improved, as a Eurasian Development Bank study describes a Central Asian grid that is often overloaded [1][4].
According to Eurasianet (October 30), Sadyr Japarov's administration will no longer issue licenses to power-hungry cryptocurrency mining farms until generation capacity improves [1].
Japarov also weighed this decision against tax revenue from mining, and demand has surged in recent weeks with the early arrival of cold weather [1].
The Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) study of the 2024 grid finds loads of 105 to 123% of permissible values [1].
The problem lies less in installed capacity than in its availability at critical hours: on December 10, 2024, about 6.6 GW of capacity in the interconnected system was unavailable or limited [1][4].
The EDB expects demand to rise by about 27% by 2030 [4].
Kyrgyzstan's energy minister met his Uzbek counterpart on October 28 to discuss supply stability [1].
The Toktogul plant supplies about 40% of Kyrgyzstan's electricity; the country had already suspended its mining farms until March 2026 because of low reservoir levels [2][5].
Key point: much of the power plants and lines date from the Soviet era, and winter is when demand soars [3].

Kyrgyzstan depends on hydropower, and therefore on its reservoir levels. Tajikistan exports power in summer but sells less in winter, when its own demand rises; the level of the Nurek plant's reservoir has dropped by 2.47 m in a year [2].
In November 2025, Kyrgyzstan had already suspended all its mining farms until March 2026; Caspian Post does not say what has happened since spring [5].
The World Bank estimates that the region's electricity demand could triple by 2050 if the trend continues [3]. The sources consulted do not specify the basis for the EDB's 27% forecast [4].
Far from home, but worth knowing: cryptocurrencies consume real electricity, and entire countries sometimes have to choose between them and heating [1][5].

Bhutan hosts a Thai prime minister for the first time in eight years

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul is in Thimphu from October 30 to November 1, a first for a head of government of his country in eight years. Three agreements are being signed (health, agricultural finance, clean energy) and free trade between the two countries is being revived [1][2][4].

Anutin Charnvirakul is making an official visit to Bhutan from October 30 to November 1, 2026, the first by a Thai prime minister in eight years, on the occasion of the 37th anniversary of diplomatic relations [1][3][4].
Talks with Bhutanese Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay took place on October 30 at the Prime Minister's Office in Thimphu [4][5].

Three agreements were signed in Thimphu on Saturday, October 31, in the presence of Anutin: health, agricultural finance and clean energy, including technical assistance for a 100 MW solar project [2][4].

The health agreement, concluded between the two countries' health ministries, covers universal health coverage, disease prevention and control, medical staff training and research; it also provides for Bhutanese patients to be treated in Thai public hospitals [4].

According to Thai government spokesperson Ekkapob Pianpises, the agreements aim to exchange know-how and technologies, improve care, open access to credit for farmers and small businesses, and support renewable energy [4].
The two leaders welcomed the free trade agreement between their countries, which they hope to see enter into force on January 1, 2027 [5].

On November 1, Anutin is due to travel to Gelephu for "Project 108", which aims to complete 108 stupas in a single day; he said other investments in this area, which has significant economic potential, should be studied [4].
Key point: Bhutan, a small Himalayan kingdom landlocked between India and China, is adding a distant Southeast Asian neighbor to its partners, and Thailand gains an unusual ally there [1][3].
The three agreements are concrete: accessible care in Thai hospitals, credit for farmers and small businesses, solar power. They affect daily life rather than diplomacy alone [2][4].

Free trade is the economic framework of the relationship: the two leaders describe it as an important mechanism for increasing trade and creating new economic opportunities, but its entry into force is only hoped for on January 1, 2027 [5].

Gelephu, which Anutin is visiting on November 1, is cited by the Thai prime minister as an area with strong potential for future investment; no specific agreement on Gelephu has been reported so far [4].

This visit changes nothing in your daily life in France. It shows how middle-sized Asian countries are forging direct agreements (health, agriculture, solar, trade) without going through the major powers, which is gradually weighing on the region's trade routes [4][5].

news.2026-10-31-allemagne-pib-t3-depense: Germany grows 0.2%, slightly better than expected, thanks to the state

The Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) published a first estimate on October 30: German GDP grew 0.2% in the third quarter, while analysts surveyed by FactSet expected 0.1%. Public spending, on defense and infrastructure, is supporting activity [1][2][3].
GDP grew 0.2% on the quarter (adjusted for prices, seasonal variations and calendar effects) and 1.3% year on year; Destatis did not revise its figures for the first two quarters [1][3].
Consumption is slightly positive, but investment is declining, according to provisional data [3].
Exports, very strong in the first half, slowed sharply in the third quarter [3].

The Bundesbank, the central bank, judged on October 21 that the economy had probably stagnated; it cited temporary factors, including the very low level of the Rhine, which restricts river transport and weighs on industry [2][4][5].

Key point: Europe's largest economy is not shrinking, but it depends heavily on government money. Chancellor Friedrich Merz launched a massive defense and infrastructure spending plan, which is supporting the economy this year [2].
The government forecasts 1.3% growth in 2026 and 1.1% in 2027 [1]. Destatis will publish the breakdown of investment, public spending and foreign trade on November 25 [3].
Germany is France's largest customer: when it holds up, French exports benefit [1][2]. But if its own exports run out of steam, its industry buys less [3].
Destatis publishes the detailed Q3 GDP results: investment, public spending, foreign trade [3].
